title: The Chariot

seo.title: Destiny matrix 7 — The Chariot: meaning of the arcanum
seo.description: Arcanum 7, The Chariot, is the energy of will, speed and victory. What 7 means in the destiny matrix: its character, its engine, its strong and weak versions.

meaning: The seventh arcanum is the energy of directed movement. If you reduce The Chariot to a single word, that word is “forward”: the number turns any task into a distance you have to cover before anyone else. What 7 means in the destiny matrix is a constant inner acceleration, where will, speed and hunger for a result are fused into one push — and that push needs a goal, or it starts to burn the person carrying it.

The inner motor of The Chariot is not ambition but the fear of stopping. Deep down lives the certainty: while I move, I am winning; the moment I stand still, I have lost. From there comes the number’s main conflict. Two forces pull the arcanum at once — the dash and the holding back — and the whole fate is decided by which of them leads. Power under control arrives first; the same power with no steering becomes a way to crash.

Being a seven is living with the motor always running. Thought outruns the conversation, a decision ripens before the details have been thought through, and other people’s calm reads as slowness. It is hard for such a person to believe that you can do nothing and still lose nothing; that feeling reaches The Chariot last of all, and usually at a high price.

The strong version of the number is gathered will: a clear goal, a chosen direction, and all the energy striking one point, so the seven gets through while others are still weighing things up. The weak version is the same power with no vector: thrill instead of sense, bravado instead of an outcome, constant tension because of everything standing in the way. The difference is not the size of the engine but whether it has a direction.

What sets The Chariot apart from its neighbours is action itself. The sixth arcanum, The Lovers, lives by choice and connection — it matters with whom and for whose sake; the seven dislikes choosing and wants to be driving already, and treats hesitation as time lost. The eighth arcanum, Justice, weighs things first: it hears both sides and only then gives its decision; The Chariot decides on the move and wins by pressure and pace. Where Justice stops to check the account, the seven pushes and overtakes.

article.title: The 7th arcanum in the destiny matrix: The Chariot
article.short: Seven in the destiny matrix is The Chariot, the arcanum of directed will. It gives you the knack of gathering yourself and your circumstances into a single movement and driving it through to victory, especially where others have already stopped. It has one weak spot, too: The Chariot wins in the outer world, but questions like “why?” and “what do I actually feel?” are not settled by speed. Below: how the seven looks in the plus and in the minus, which plot it keeps replaying, which points and tails it turns up in, and what Waite wrote about it.

seo.title: Destiny matrix 7: The Chariot — meaning, program, karmic tail
seo.description: Destiny matrix 7 is The Chariot, will with a direction: its plus and minus, how to break the loop of program 7, four karmic tails and the 7 in a couple.

sections.h2: What 7 means in the destiny matrix
paragraphs: The Chariot is the seventh of the 22 major arcana, and its meaning fits into a short formula: will with a direction. Plenty of arcana have energy; what sets the seven apart is a course. A person with a strong 7 can name a goal, gather time, money, people and themselves around it — and get there.

The Chariot does not move because everything inside agrees. “I want” and “I’m scared”, “I must” and “I don’t feel like it”, calculation and resentment all pull in different directions, and the seven can make the parts that disagree move one way. Its strength is steering a contradiction, not living without one. That is why these people often find their footing in a crisis: when everything falls apart for others, they finally have a job to do.

For the seven, the road is never sightseeing. Benebell Wen, author of Holistic Tarot, describes The Chariot as “travel not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition”. Moving for a job, a business trip to close a deal, a climb to the summit — the seven always travels to fetch something.

In the deck, The Chariot comes straight after The Lovers (6): there you choose, here you drive on the choice. The seventh arcanum is a decision already being carried out, with all its pluses (things are moving) and minuses (it is too late for doubts).

Arthur Edward Waite, whose design lies behind the best-known tarot deck, singled out two things in this card, and the whole of the seven in the matrix rests on them. First, the victory is won, not handed down: the hero of the card, in his words, “is not hereditary royalty and he is not priesthood”. Second, the victory belongs to the outer world and the mind, and it does not yet mean the victor has mastered himself. The seven’s standing is earned; its weak spot lies within.

**In short.** The strength: carrying things through to a result. The weakness: not knowing how to stop and not seeing the cost. The task: knowing in advance where you are going and what will count as arriving.

sections.h2: Seven in the plus and in the minus
paragraphs: The same energy in different hands looks like leadership or like a battering ram. Here is how to tell them apart in everyday life.

head: Where it shows
In the plus
In the minus
rows: Decisions
Decides fast once the goal is clear and does not reopen the decision at every step
Decides before understanding the goal, then defends the decision like territory
Work
Finishes what others gave up on; strong at launches, crunch time, moves and competitions
Takes on five things and drops them halfway; measures life by a speed report
Arguments
Speaks plainly, takes a hit, stands up for their own
Wins the argument and loses the person; won’t give way even on trifles
Closeness
Pulls the couple forward, acts when someone close is struggling
Treats feelings as problems to solve; the partner rides along as a passenger nobody asked
Rest
Recharges through movement: the road, sport, a change of scene
A pause feels like losing; a holiday turns into an itinerary
Money
Earns on results: a project, a deal, a percentage
Rushes, takes risks, borrows for the next push

paragraphs: The seven’s minus comes in two kinds, and they are easy to mistake for different arcana. The first is the overheated Chariot: it drives, presses, flattens, abandons. The second is the Chariot stuck in park: there is no goal, the power has nowhere to go and turns into irritation, nitpicking and quarrels out of nothing. From outside the second one looks like laziness, but it is an engine without a road. Both have the same way out — a goal worth travelling for, not the ride itself.

Even in Waite’s old fortune-telling list, The Chariot puts “succour, providence” right next to “war, presumption, vengeance”. It is one power: turned towards people, it comes to the rescue; turned against them, it goes to war.

The most interesting thing about the seven shows not in its victories but in what victory cannot take. Waite describes the hero of the card as a triumph of the mind: he is “conquest on all planes — in the mind, in science, in progress”. Then he spends almost a whole paragraph listing where that victory runs out. Here are three of Waite’s points that are easy to recognise in life.

**Solves problems, not mysteries.** In Waite, the victor answers the riddles of Nature but not the questions of Grace. In everyday terms: the seven is strong wherever a problem yields to effort — pass, build, move, win, pull someone out. And it is lost where there is nothing to solve: grief, falling in love, faith, forgiveness. Someone close is crying, and five minutes later they are handed a three-point plan. The plan is good. The person was not waiting for a plan.

**Frees others, stays captive himself.** Another of Waite’s caveats: the liberation the victor brings “may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding”. A familiar picture: someone has pulled a brother out of debt, moved their parents, rescued a colleague’s deadline, and when asked “but what do you want?”, answers with a to-do list for the week.

**The crown has to be won again.** Waite writes that The Chariot is really “the King in his triumph”: the victory that creates kingship as its natural consequence, unlike the vested crown of The Emperor (4). Hence the seven’s particular feeling: respect does not keep, it has to be earned again every time. The Emperor can sit on the throne. The Chariot, to stay itself, has to keep moving, and that is at once its gift and its trap.

Wen adds a psychological detail. She links the card to the sign of Cancer: “tough on the outside, but deep down… quite vulnerable and sensitive”. Such a person likes to appear in control, yet has two habitual escapes from anything hard — to run from the problem, or to attack it with such aggression that the real conversation never has to happen. The third way — staying and talking it through — is the hardest and the most grown-up for the seven.
A mature seven does not slow down. It learns to tell the problems that need winning from the questions that need living through.

sections.h2: Where the seven stands and what it does there
paragraphs: The seven is no rarity: 81.2% of people have it somewhere in their reading. So what matters is not the fact but the place: The Chariot in the calling card, in the centre and on the money line says different things. The shares below are counted over every date of birth from 1900 to 2026.

The first impression is of someone already on their way somewhere: composed, to the point, quick to act. They are remembered for what they did, not for what they said
Spiritual task — born in July
Will comes as an assignment: learn to aim it rather than spend it on everything at once. This point also opens the talent line — [the seven in talents](/encyclopedia/position/profession/7)

Money channel; the “dollar” point of other charts — the middle of the money line
26.8%; the “dollar” point — 6.2%

Purpose: personal, social, planetary
To get through where others stopped, and to lead those who would never have dared on their own

Ten years of movement: relocations, career leaps, a business of one’s own. For those born on the 7th or the 25th it is the first ten years of life, for July births from 20 to 30, for a 7 in the birth year from 40 to 50, for a 7 in the karmic task from 60 to 70
Personal year
A breakthrough year: what had stalled starts moving, and you set the route. [The seven as your year](/year/7)

paragraphs: Where the seven never appears: at the entry of relationships and the tail, and in the spiritual purpose. Only multiples of three stand in these two points, so The Chariot cannot get there.

Two common mix-ups. Born on the 16th? That is not a seven: in the matrix, numbers up to 22 are not reduced, and 16 stays The Tower. And a “life path number 7” from classic numerology is a different calculation with a different meaning: it does not mean you have The Chariot in your matrix.

sections.h2: Program 7 in the destiny matrix: The Chariot’s loop
paragraphs: When people ask about “program 7”, they mean the seven in a karmic point — where an arcanum describes not a character trait but a plot that keeps replaying by itself. In the reading, the programs section looks at the karmic task, the centre of the chart and the spiritual purpose; the seven can stand in the first two, and does for one person in five (20.6%). In the karmic tail it appears for 14%, and the two groups partly overlap: the last number of the tail is the karmic task itself. How programs work in general is covered [in the article on programs](/programs); here is what the loop looks like for The Chariot.

ol: **The challenge.** Someone said “you won’t make it”, “it’s impossible”, “you can’t do it”. Or the challenge is self-made: a deadline, a record, a new city.
**Mobilisation.** Everything that does not serve the goal is put off until later: sleep, loved ones, conversations, your own tiredness.
**Victory.** It worked, and often better than for anyone else.
**Emptiness.** The joy of the finish does not last until morning. Recognition does not hold, the people around are worn out, and everything that was put off presents its bill.
**A new challenge.** Stopping feels like disappearing, and the loop starts over.

paragraphs: The loop has two common variations. In the first there is no finish at all: start, push, new idea, abandoned halfway, next start. In the second there is no race: a person with a strong seven gets stuck without a goal and fights whoever is nearby — out of boredom, not malice.

paragraphs.h3: Program or character: how to tell

paragraphs: Speed and drive on their own are not a program. It is a program when the ending is the same across different people and circumstances: alone at the finish again, “I’ll rest when it’s done” again, loved ones the last to hear about the decision again. And when stopping does not work, even though you badly want to.
The loop is most often set off by:

ul: someone else’s “no” or “you won’t make it”;
waiting on something that does not depend on you;
a situation where someone else holds the wheel;
an empty week with nothing to tackle;
a feeling that cannot be solved — your own or someone else’s.

ol: **The finish before the start.** Before something new, write down what will count as arriving: a sum, a date, a result. Once you arrive, stop, even if you still have strength left.
**One race at a time.** Something new begins when the old thing is finished or honestly closed, not dropped.
**Three days after a win.** Don’t start the next thing until you have lived through this finish: mark it, tell someone about it, notice what you feel.
**Match your pace to your fellow travellers.** Before a push, ask those it affects whether they are coming with you, and at what speed.
**Don’t fix — be there.** When someone close is struggling, the first ten minutes go without advice.
**Don’t run, don’t attack.** In a hard conversation, notice the two habitual exits — escaping into tasks or going on the offensive — and choose the third: stay and talk it through.

paragraphs: The speed does not go anywhere — what changes is what it is spent on. How the programs section reads in a specific chart is shown [on the section page](/encyclopedia/position/loops).

sections.h2: The seven in the karmic tail
paragraphs: The karmic tail is three arcana at the bottom of the chart, read in order: entry, mechanism and root. The seven turns up in the tail for 14% of people, but only in two places out of three. It never stands first: only multiples of three appear at the entry of the tail. So there are just four tails with a seven.

head: Tail
Where the seven is
How often
What it is about
rows: [12-19-7](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/12-19-7)
root
9.3%, about one in eleven
The “Warrior”: life on a war footing — sacrifice for the cause, glory, the next war
[3-7-22](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/3-7-22)
mechanism
The “Prisoner”: a warm home turns into walls, the person fights their way out and builds the same walls in the new place
[21-7-13](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/21-7-13)
mechanism
The victor conquers their world, sees it does not match the plan, and cuts it down; the task is to learn to finish rather than destroy
[21-10-7](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/21-10-7)
root
0.3%, one in three hundred
The “Warrior of Faith”: a picture of how the world should be runs into life’s turns; the task is to turn faith into a road

paragraphs: When the seven is at the root of the tail, it is the task: learning to steer your own movement instead of fighting. When it is in the middle, it is the mechanism, the way the loop spins up: a push, an escape or an attack.

Popular readings tie a seven in the tail to a soldier’s past life: you were a soldier and died far from home. That is a belief of the school, not a conclusion from the card. The Chariot itself speaks of today’s script — the habit of taking everything by force, even what you could simply have asked for. How to read the tail as a whole is covered [in the karmic tail guide](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail).

sections.h2: The seven in a couple: two matrices, one compatibility
paragraphs: A search for “7 in compatibility” is usually about the compatibility matrix. It is calculated like this: add up the matching points of two personal matrices and reduce each sum to a number from 1 to 22. The result is a third matrix — a portrait of the union. Below is how Yuliana Lisovskaya, author of a book on destiny matrix compatibility, reads the seven in such a matrix; the wording is ours, the meaning is hers.

**In the centre of the compatibility matrix**, that is, in the general atmosphere, the seven makes the union a team on the move. Each partner has their own work and their own growth; together there are relocations, hikes, shared projects, and at the start a strong passion. For all that activity, the couple needs discipline and clear roles inside, or the movement turns into bustle.

**In the point that shows the couple from outside**, the seven draws people who are taken for friends and comrades rather than lovers: always ready to go, often moving house, as if looking for their home.

**In the couple’s tasks**, the seven means a contest for the lead, control, an imbalance between career and relationship, decisions made in the heat of the moment, and a demand that the other give up their own goals for “shared” ones that are in fact someone else’s.
**In money**, such a couple earns well and can run a business together, but the budget is safer in one pair of hands: if both pull on the wheel, this is the area that suffers.

The seven’s minus in a couple, as in a personal matrix, comes in two kinds. Active: they grab at everything and drop it, rush, take risks. Passive: the passion fades, there is no goal, and the two drag each other down. This system gives no compatibility percentages: the seven in a couple tells you not whether you are a match, but what the union rests on and where it breaks.

If the seven stands in your partner’s personal matrix, you will get movement and protection beside them, and they need a road of their own and respect for it. What the seven brings to relationships is covered [on a separate page](/encyclopedia/position/relations/7).

sections.h2: Arcanum 7 in men and in women
paragraphs: Gender recalculates nothing in the matrix: a man and a woman born on the same day have the same numbers, and The Chariot means the same thing for both — will with a direction. The difference is not in the chart but in how the people around meet the same power.

Where drive is praised, the seven’s trap is a race nobody stops until it is too late. Where the same drive is called abrasive, the trap is different: spending energy on apologising for your own speed. Which of the two is yours depends on how you were met, not on your gender. The advice to “tone it down” helps in neither case: the seven needs not less force but a chosen route.

The Emperor holds what already exists, The Chariot conquers. Waite says so outright: a victory that creates kingship, not a vested crown

The Hierophant’s authority comes from tradition and initiation, the seven’s from results

paragraphs: If the seven sits next to one of these cards in your chart, look at the combination pages — for example, [with The Emperor](/encyclopedia/combination/4-7), [with Strength](/encyclopedia/combination/7-11), [with The Wheel of Fortune](/encyclopedia/combination/7-10) or [with The Fool](/encyclopedia/combination/7-22).

sections.h2: Waite’s Chariot: tarot card VII in the classic deck
paragraphs: The best-known image of The Chariot is Pamela Colman Smith’s drawing for the Waite deck (1909). Everything below refers to that card.

ul: An “erect and princely figure”, in Waite’s words, stands in a chariot under a canopy strewn with stars.
On his head is a crown with an eight-pointed star; on his breastplate, a square.
Crescent moons on his shoulders. Waite cautiously says these “are supposed to be the Urim and Thummim” — in the Bible, the sacred lots of the high priest, used to ask the will of heaven.
His belt and skirt are covered with signs; Wen finds them “reminiscent of alchemy and astrology”.
In his right hand is a wand. In the book Waite says the hero is “carrying a drawn sword”, but there is no sword on Smith’s card: text and picture part ways here.
There are no reins. Nothing ties the chariot to the creatures that draw it.
In front lie two sphinxes, one black and one white.
On the front of the car are a winged disc and a shield with a sign in which Wen sees the lingam and yoni, the male and female principles: a union of outer and inner rule.
Behind him are a walled city and a river.

paragraphs: Waite explains the sphinxes by the riddle the victor has solved: “He has thus replied to the sphinx.” In older decks the chariot was drawn by horses — white ones in the eighteenth century, and in some versions a lion and a leopard. The sphinxes, as Waite himself admits, were a later invention, devised “to support a particular historical hypothesis”, and he took the variant from Éliphas Lévi for the sake of its symbolism. Wen puts a question to the picture: “who exactly is in control, the sphinxes or the charioteer?” There are no reins on the card, so the question is not idle: the chariot holds together by will alone, and the moment that will slackens, the black and the white will pull in different directions.

Of the hero himself Waite speaks in the words of the Psalm: “He has led captivity captive.” This is conquest on all planes — in the mind, in science, in progress, in certain trials of initiation — and “above all things triumph in the mind”. Five limits follow. The question of the sphinx is a Mystery of Nature, not of the world of Grace, and to Grace the charioteer could offer no answer. What he has conquered is manifest and external, not within himself. Setting others free, he may remain in the bondage of logic. The tests of initiation he passed are to be understood physically or rationally. And if he came to the pillars of the Temple between which the High Priestess sits, he could not open her scroll called Tora, nor answer if she questioned him. “He is not hereditary royalty and he is not priesthood.”

In the historical part of the book Waite explains the name: “the lesser stands for the greater”, and the card is really “the King in his triumph” — a victory that creates kingship as its natural consequence, unlike the vested royalty of the fourth card. Court de Gébelin saw in it Osiris Triumphing, the spring sun that has overcome the obstacles of winter; Waite rejects that reading.
In the third part of the book Waite gives a short list of fortune-telling meanings.

ul: **Upright:** succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble.
**Reversed:** riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat.

paragraphs: There are no reversed cards in the destiny matrix: a number calculated from a date does not lie upside down. The seven’s hard side is the same power gone off course, not a “reversed Chariot”.
The Chariot has the same number in every system: VII in Waite, in the Marseille deck and in the matrix. There is none of the confusion that surrounds Strength and Justice, which Waite swapped round.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922), illustrations by Pamela Colman Smith: Part I, § 2; Part II, § 2; Part III, § 3. Quotations are in Waite’s original wording.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 9, Key 7 — The Chariot, with the author’s errata taken into account.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility) (2024), the section on the 7th energy.
The calculation follows Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme. The shares of people were counted by going through all 46,299 dates from 1 January 1900 to 5 October 2026.

paragraphs: The destiny matrix is a system of self-knowledge: it describes tendencies and recurring scenarios, not events and not other people’s actions.
